steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP / computational social science paper on how US Yelp reviews (and LLM-generated reviews) frame immigrant cuisines — othering and low-status framing. Motivate it, cover gaps in prior work, state our research questions and the sociological theories behind our hypotheses, and summarize the findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why implicit attitudes toward food matter; stereotypes and LLMs
- Limitations of prior work
- Our study and research questions (Q1–Q3)
- Theory behind Q1: cultural omnivorousness, othering
- Theory behind Q2: ethnic succession of taste, status; hypotheses H1–H3
- Data and findings
- Implications

steps.name: detailed_outline

  - online corpora train LLMs that generate all kinds of text -> important to understand harms there
- Prior work limitations
  - coarse signals like numerical ratings (cite); review language in small datasets (cite)
  - larger studies ignore restaurant/neighborhood factors (price point, neighborhood racial diversity) confounded with sentiment (cite)
  - naive word counts; stinky restaurant vs. stinky tofu (Chinese dish)
- Our study
  - framing in 2.1M English Yelp reviews; NLP parsing; control for restaurant quality + neighborhood demographics (Figure 1)
  - LLM stereotypes via controlled review-generation task
  - Q1 immigrant vs non-immigrant framing (immigrant = cuisine based outside US)
  - Q2 more vs less assimilated immigrant groups
  - Q3 do LLMs transmit same disparities as Yelp reviewers
- Q1 theory
  - sociology of taste; cultural omnivorousness: immigrant food climbing in status, broader shift (e.g., music) from few highbrow genres to democratic variety (cite)
  - enabled by framing as exotic and authentic: novel + authentic -> legitimize omnivorous palate beyond haute cuisine, keep discerning taste vs indiscriminate appetite (cite)
  - exoticism, authenticity = harmful "othering" (cite); outsider consumption, objectifies food, reductive, essentializing
- Q2 theory + hypotheses
  - ethnic succession of taste: status differences from migration patterns, socioeconomic gaps
  - Italian immigration slowed in 20th century, Italian Americans moved up, so did Italian food; Asian, Hispanic food lower status, ongoing immigration into low-wage jobs esp. restaurants (cite)
  - like class distinctions elsewhere: highbrow -> aesthetic, emotional judgments; lowbrow -> functional, material criteria (cite)
  - culinary: hygiene and cost (cite)
  - discourse others immigrant cuisines, devalues less assimilated ethnicities
  - LLMs trained on online discourse similar; representational harms work, e.g. (cite)
  - H1 othered: exotic H1a, prototypical H1b, authentic H1c
  - H2 more assimilated -> luxury H2a; less assimilated -> cost H2b, hygiene H2c
  - H3 LLMs reproduce differences
- Data and findings
  - 2.1M reviews, 14 US states; control price, star rating
  - three largest sources: European (Eur), Asian (As), Latin American (Lat)
  - evidence for all 3: immigrant -> authentic overwhelmingly; only As, Lat -> exotic
  - As, Lat more authentic in zipcodes with fewer Asian/Hispanic residents -> othering driven by cultural outsiders
  - As, Lat -> cheap and dirty vs Eur; persists even at $$$-$$$$ (4 tiers: $, $$, $$$, $$$$); culinary glass ceiling (cite)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Identifying and understanding implicit attitudes toward food is important for trying to mitigate social prejudice, because food plays a pervasive role as a marker of cultural and ethnic identity. Stereotypes about cuisines are a kind of representational harm. They contribute to racialized public discourse, and in turn they may perpetuate prejudice toward ethnic groups and hurt restaurants' economic outcomes. For example in the United States Chinese food is often associated with dirty kitchens and cheap takeout, and French food is associated with upscale dining. It is especially important to understand representational harms in online corpora, since these corpora are used to train large language models (LLMs), and LLMs are more and more used to generate all kinds of texts.

Prior work on attitudes to immigrant food used coarser signals like numerical restaurant ratings, or studied review language in smaller datasets. Larger-scale studies on the other hand ignored factors related to the restaurant and neighborhood (e.g., price point, neighborhood racial diversity) that may be confounded with review sentiment. Also, prior studies relied on naive methods based on word counts that don't distinguish between uses in different contexts, e.g., a stinky restaurant vs. the stinky tofu (which is the name of a Chinese dish).

We build on previous work by studying framing in 2.1M English language Yelp reviews. We use NLP parsing techniques to do careful linguistic analysis of how customers evaluate restaurants, and we control for restaurant quality and neighborhood demographics (Figure 1). Also, LLMs are more and more used to generate reviews and all kinds of texts, so we investigate whether human stereotypes persist in LLMs with a controlled review-generation task. Our research questions are:

- Q1 Framing of immigrant vs. non-immigrant food: How are immigrant restaurants (i.e. those identified with a cuisine based outside the US) framed compared to non-immigrant restaurants?

- Q1 theory
  - cultural omnivorousness: immigrant food climbing in status; broader shift (e.g., music) from few highbrow genres to democratic variety
  - exotic + authentic framing legitimizes omnivorous palate beyond haute cuisine, keeps pretense of discerning taste
  - exoticism, authenticity = harmful "othering"; objectifies food, reductive, essentializing
- Q2 theory + hypotheses
  - ethnic succession of taste; Italian food rose with Italian Americans in 20th century; Asian, Hispanic food lower status (low-wage jobs, restaurant industry)
  - highbrow -> aesthetic/emotional judgments; lowbrow -> functional/material; culinary: hygiene, cost
  - LLMs trained on online discourse expected to be similar (representational harms work)
  - H1 (exotic H1a, prototypical H1b, authentic H1c); H2 (luxury H2a; cost H2b, hygiene H2c); H3 LLMs reproduce
- Data and findings
  - 2.1M reviews, 14 US states; control price, star rating; Eur, As, Lat
  - immigrant -> authentic; only As, Lat -> exotic; more authentic in zipcodes with fewer Asian/Hispanic residents
  - As, Lat cheap and dirty vs Eur, even at $$$-$$$$ (4 tiers: $, $$, $$$, $$$$); culinary glass ceiling
  - GPT-3.5 similar disparities
- Implications
  - corroborate theories; downstream harms in LLMs; dictionaries + methods for other domains

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Identifying and understanding implicit attitudes toward food is important for trying to mitigate social prejudice, because food plays a pervasive role as a marker of cultural and ethnic identity. Stereotypes about cuisines are a kind of representational harm. They contribute to racialized public discourse, and in turn they may perpetuate prejudice toward ethnic groups and hurt restaurants' economic outcomes. For example in the United States Chinese food is often associated with dirty kitchens and cheap takeout, and French food is associated with upscale dining. It is especially important to understand representational harms in online corpora, since these corpora are used to train large language models (LLMs), and LLMs are more and more used to generate all kinds of texts.

Prior work on attitudes to immigrant food used coarser signals like numerical restaurant ratings, or studied review language in smaller datasets. Larger-scale studies on the other hand ignored factors related to the restaurant and neighborhood (e.g., price point, neighborhood racial diversity) that may be confounded with review sentiment. Also, prior studies relied on naive methods based on word counts that don't distinguish between uses in different contexts, e.g., a stinky restaurant vs. the stinky tofu (which is the name of a Chinese dish).

We build on previous work by studying framing in 2.1M English language Yelp reviews. We use NLP parsing techniques to do careful linguistic analysis of how customers evaluate restaurants, and we control for restaurant quality and neighborhood demographics (Figure 1). Also, LLMs are more and more used to generate reviews and all kinds of texts, so we investigate whether human stereotypes persist in LLMs with a controlled review-generation task. Our research questions are:

- Q1 Framing of immigrant vs. non-immigrant food: How are immigrant restaurants (i.e. those identified with a cuisine based outside the US) framed compared to non-immigrant restaurants?

- Q2 Framing within immigrant foods: Are cuisines of more assimilated immigrant groups framed differently from those of less assimilated groups?

- Q3 Framing in synthetic reviews: Do LLMs transmit the same framing disparities as Yelp reviewers?

These questions come from work in the sociology of taste. For Q1, the theory of cultural omnivorousness says that immigrant food is climbing in social status. This is part of a broader shift today that also happens in other forms of cultural consumption (e.g., music), from a small number of highbrow genres to a more democratic variety. The important thing is that this shift is enabled by perceiving and framing immigrant food as exotic and authentic. Consumers valorize immigrant food as novel, and as authentically novel, so they can legitimize choosing a more omnivorous palate beyond traditional haute cuisine but still keep a pretense of discerning taste and not an indiscriminate appetite. But the frames of exoticism and authenticity are also harmful forms of "othering". They reinforce an outsider mode of cultural consumption that objectifies food in reductive and essentializing ways.

For Q2, the theory of the ethnic succession of taste says that cuisines have status differences because of migration patterns and the socioeconomic gaps that result. For example Italian immigration to the US slowed in the 20th century and Italian Americans moved up the socioeconomic ladder, and the status of Italian food went up too. On the other hand Asian and Hispanic food are still lower status, because ongoing Asian and Hispanic immigration keeps filling low-wage jobs, especially in the restaurant industry. These status differences look like class distinctions in other domains of cultural consumption. Highbrow genres usually get aesthetic and emotional judgments, and lowbrow genres are evaluated on functional and material criteria. For food, the latter means a concern for hygiene and cost. So together these theories describe US food review discourse as othering immigrant cuisines and devaluing the cuisines of less assimilated ethnicities. And we expect LLMs that are trained on online discourse data to show similar tendencies, which fits with work on representational harms, e.g.,. So our hypotheses are:

- H1 Immigrant restaurants are othered (i.e. framed as more exotic H1a, prototypical H1b, and authentic H1c) compared to non-immigrant restaurants.

- H2 Restaurants associated with more assimilated immigrant groups are framed in high status terms of luxury H2a; conversely, restaurants of less assimilated groups are framed in low status terms of cost H2b and hygiene H2c.

- H3 LLMs reproduce the same framing differences as Yelp reviewers.

To test the hypotheses we use 2.1M reviews of restaurants in 14 US states, and we control for things like restaurant price and star rating. We focus on the three biggest sources of immigrant food in the US: European cuisine (Eur), Asian cuisine (As), and Latin American cuisine (Lat).

We find evidence for all 3 sets of hypotheses. Immigrant restaurants are much more likely to be described as authentic, but only As and Lat are more likely to be described as exotic. We also find that As and Lat are framed as more authentic in zipcodes with fewer Asian and Hispanic residents, respectively. This suggests that othering may be driven by cultural outsiders and not by the members of an ethnic group themselves.

Reviewers are also more likely to describe As and Lat as cheap and dirty compared to Eur. These disparities are still there even for the most expensive $$$-$$$$ restaurants (Yelp puts restaurants into 4 tiers based on menu prices: $, $$, $$$, $$$$). This supports the idea of a culinary glass ceiling that keeps the cuisines of less assimilated non-European immigrants from getting the same status as the European ones.

Last, we find that GPT-3.5 shows framing disparities similar to human consumers: immigrant cuisines get more othering and non-European immigrant cuisines get more low status framing.

Overall our results corroborate social theories about racialized evaluative processes and the systematic devaluation of cuisines associated with non-white groups, and they show downstream harms in LLMs. Our dictionaries and methods can also be used in other domains of cultural consumption to study how immigrant cultures are perceived in our more and more globalized society.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Identifying and understanding implicit attitudes toward food is important for efforts to mitigate social prejudice, given food's pervasive role as a marker of cultural and ethnic identity. Stereotypes about cuisines are a form of representational harm that contributes to racialized public discourse and may in turn perpetuate prejudice toward ethnic groups and negatively affect restaurants' economic outcomes [1,2]. For example, in the United States, Chinese food is commonly associated with dirty kitchens and cheap takeout, whereas French food is associated with upscale dining [3,4]. Understanding representational harms in online corpora is especially important, since these corpora are used to train large language models (LLMs) that are increasingly used to generate texts of all kinds.

Prior work on attitudes toward immigrant food has used coarser-grained signals such as numerical restaurant ratings [4] or studied review language in smaller scale datasets [5,6,7,8]. Meanwhile, larger-scale studies have ignored restaurant and neighborhood-related factors (e.g., price point, neighborhood racial diversity) that may be confounded with review sentiment [9,10]. Moreover, prior studies have relied on naive word-count-based methods that do not distinguish between contextually different uses, e.g., a stinky restaurant vs. the stinky tofu (the name of a Chinese dish).

We build on previous work through a study of framing in 2.1M English language Yelp reviews, using NLP parsing techniques for careful linguistic analysis of how customers evaluate restaurants while controlling for restaurant quality and neighborhood demographics (Figure 1). Since LLMs are increasingly used to generate reviews and texts of all kinds, we also investigate the persistence of human stereotypes in LLMs through a controlled review-generation task. Our research questions are as follows:

- Q1 Framing of immigrant vs. non-immigrant food: How are immigrant restaurants (i.e. those identified with a cuisine based outside the US) framed compared to non-immigrant restaurants?

- Q2 Framing within immigrant foods: Are cuisines of more assimilated immigrant groups framed differently from those of less assimilated groups?

- Q3 Framing in synthetic reviews: Do LLMs transmit the same framing disparities as Yelp reviewers?

These questions are informed by work in the sociology of taste. Regarding Q1, the theory of cultural omnivorousness holds that immigrant food is climbing in social status, as part of a broader contemporary shift in other forms of cultural consumption (e.g., music) from a small number of highbrow genres to a more democratic variety [11]. Crucially, this shift is enabled by perceiving and framing immigrant food as exotic and authentic: by valorizing immigrant food as novel, and authentically so, consumers can legitimize a more omnivorous palate beyond traditional haute cuisine while still maintaining a pretense of discerning taste rather than an indiscriminate appetite [5]. At the same time, the frames of exoticism and authenticity are harmful forms of "othering" [12] that reinforce an outsider mode of cultural consumption, objectifying food in reductive and essentializing ways.

Regarding Q2, the theory of the ethnic succession of taste argues that status differences among cuisines arise from migration patterns and the resulting socioeconomic gaps. E.g., as Italian immigration to the US slowed in the 20th century and Italian Americans moved up the socioeconomic ladder, the status of Italian food rose too; conversely, Asian and Hispanic food remain lower status, since ongoing Asian and Hispanic immigration continues to fill low-wage jobs, especially in the restaurant industry [4,13]. These status differences mirror class distinctions in other domains of cultural consumption: highbrow genres tend to receive aesthetic and emotional judgments, while lowbrow genres are evaluated on functional and material criteria [14,15,16]. In a culinary context, the latter becomes a concern for hygiene and cost [17,10,18,15,8]. Together, these theories describe a US food review discourse that others immigrant cuisines and devalues those of less assimilated ethnicities. Finally, we expect LLMs trained on online discourse data to show similar tendencies, in line with work on representational harms, e.g., [19,20]. Our hypotheses are therefore:

- H1 Immigrant restaurants are othered (i.e. framed as more exotic H1a, prototypical H1b, and authentic H1c) compared to non-immigrant restaurants.

- H2 Restaurants associated with more assimilated immigrant groups are framed in high status terms of luxury H2a; conversely, restaurants of less assimilated groups are framed in low status terms of cost H2b and hygiene H2c.

- H3 LLMs reproduce the same framing differences as Yelp reviewers.

We test our hypotheses on 2.1M reviews of restaurants in 14 US states, controlling for factors such as restaurant price and star rating. We focus on the three largest sources of immigrant food in the US: European cuisine (Eur), Asian cuisine (As), and Latin American cuisine (Lat).

We find evidence for all 3 sets of hypotheses: immigrant restaurants are overwhelmingly more likely to be described as authentic, although only As and Lat are more likely to be described as exotic. We also find that As and Lat are framed as more authentic in zipcodes with fewer Asian and Hispanic residents, respectively, which suggests that othering may be driven by cultural outsiders rather than by members of an ethnic group themselves.

In addition, reviewers are more likely to describe As and Lat as cheap and dirty compared to Eur. These disparities persist even for the most expensive $$$-$$$$ restaurants (Yelp sorts restaurants into 4 tiers based on menu prices: $, $$, $$$, $$$$), supporting the idea of a culinary glass ceiling that prevents the cuisines of less assimilated non-European immigrants from reaching the same status as their European counterparts [13].

Finally, we find that GPT-3.5 shows framing disparities similar to those of human consumers, with immigrant cuisines subject to more othering and non-European immigrant cuisines receiving more low status framing.

Together, our results corroborate social theories about racialized evaluative processes and the systematic devaluation of non-white associated cuisines, and they demonstrate downstream harms in LLMs. Our dictionaries and methods can also be applied to other domains of cultural consumption to study perceptions of immigrant cultures in our increasingly globalized society.
